drug_class: Proteasome inhibitor (a type of targeted cancer medicine)
purpose: Bortezomib is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, mainly multiple myeloma and a type of lymphoma called mantle cell lymphoma. It helps slow down or stop the growth of cancer cells in your body. Your doctor may use it alone or combined with other cancer medicines.
how_it_works: Your body's cells have a built-in system called a proteasome that acts like a trash disposal — it breaks down old or damaged proteins inside cells. Bortezomib blocks this trash disposal system specifically in cancer cells, causing harmful proteins to build up inside them until the cancer cells die. Because cancer cells rely on this system more heavily than normal cells, bortezomib can target them more directly.
common_side_effects: Tiredness and weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, decreased appetite, tingling, numbness or pain in the hands and feet (called peripheral neuropathy), low blood cell counts (which can increase infection risk or cause bruising and bleeding), and low blood pressure when standing up.
warnings: Bortezomib can lower your blood counts, making it easier to get infections or bleed — report any fever, chills, or unusual bruising right away. It can cause nerve damage in your hands and feet; tell your doctor immediately if you feel new or worsening numbness or pain. It may cause serious lung, heart, or liver problems in some people. Avoid live vaccines during treatment. This medicine can harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during and after treatment.
typical_dosing: Bortezomib is given as an injection either under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital. A common schedule is twice a week for two weeks, followed by a 10-day rest period — this makes up one treatment cycle. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule based on your specific condition and how well you tolerate the medicine.
